publisher: Tri Dao et al. · Stanford University
title: FlashAttention: attention is slow because of data movement, not math; tiling keeps the exact result
summary: FlashAttention doesn't change what attention computes, only how it runs on the GPU: it splits the computation into blocks that fit in on-chip SRAM, uses online softmax to recover the exact result, and never writes the N × N matrix to HBM. We hand-run the block softmax, unpack why doing more arithmetic can be faster, and walk through the training speedups and long-context experiments.
ai_summary: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness (Dao et al., Stanford University, 2022) shows that attention on GPUs is limited mainly by HBM reads and writes. It proposes an IO-aware exact attention algorithm: Q, K, and V are loaded into on-chip SRAM in blocks, online softmax merges the blocks into the exact result, and the backward pass recomputes instead of storing the attention matrix—all fused into a single CUDA kernel with provably fewer HBM accesses. In experiments, BERT-large trains 15% faster than the MLPerf 1.1 record, GPT-2 end-to-end is up to 3× faster, and memory grows linearly with sequence length, letting Transformers beat chance on Path-X and Path-256 for the first time.
brief: Problem: attention is bottlenecked by HBM reads and writes; standard implementations repeatedly read and write a large N × N matrix. Approximate attention saves compute but is often not much faster.
Method: tile blocks into on-chip SRAM, use online softmax to assemble the exact result, recompute instead of storing in the backward pass, and fuse everything into one kernel.
Results: GPT-2 attention is 7.6× faster and end-to-end up to 3× faster; BERT is 15% faster than the MLPerf record; memory grows linearly; supports 16K–64K sequences.
Limitations: every attention variant needs its own hand-written CUDA kernel; single-GPU only; some speedup numbers are inconsistent across sections.

paper.title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
paper.authors: Tri Dao, Daniel Y. Fu, Stefano Ermon, Atri Rudra, Christopher Ré

cover.headline: FlashAttention explained
cover.highlight: Slow from data movement, not math

sections.h: The bottom line: what this paper actually does

blocks.p: In May 2022, Tri Dao, Daniel Y. Fu, Stefano Ermon, and Christopher Ré of Stanford, along with Atri Rudra of the University at Buffalo, released this paper. It does not invent a new kind of attention—the output is **exactly the same** as standard attention. What it changes is how that computation runs on a GPU.

The starting point is an overlooked fact: on modern GPUs, attention is slow not mainly because of all the multiplications, but because data moves back and forth too much between the GPU's large main memory (HBM) and the chip's small on-chip cache (SRAM). Standard implementations write the entire N × N attention matrix back to HBM, read it again to apply softmax, write it again, then read it again to multiply by V. Once sequences get long, that matrix becomes the dominant cost.

FlashAttention's approach is **tiling**: split Q, K, and V into small blocks, load them into SRAM, compute one block of attention entirely on-chip, then use a small trick to assemble the per-block softmax into the correct global result. The N × N matrix never gets written to HBM. The backward pass doesn't store it either; it recomputes it on the fly from two small saved statistics.

The result: slightly more arithmetic, but far fewer HBM reads and writes, so it runs faster and uses less memory. The paper's numbers: GPT-2 attention computation is 7.6× faster; BERT-large training is 15% faster than the MLPerf 1.1 record; GPT-2 end-to-end training is up to 3× faster than the Hugging Face implementation; memory grows linearly with sequence length instead of quadratically, allowing Transformers to beat random guessing for the first time on Path-X (16K) and Path-256 (64K).

callout.title: One-sentence version
callout.text: Attention's bottleneck is moving data, not doing math. Cut the computation into blocks that fit in on-chip memory, compute each block in cache and write back only the result, then use a self-correcting softmax to assemble the blocks into an exact answer: same result, far fewer HBM accesses.

callout.title: Three small ideas you need before reading
callout.text: Don't worry if you're unfamiliar with them; these three are enough:
list: **The three attention steps**: S = QK^{⊺} computes pairwise similarity, P = softmax(S) turns each row into weights that sum to 1, and O = PV computes a weighted average. See our Transformer explainer for details.

**softmax**: turns a row of numbers into probabilities: exponentiate each number, then divide by the sum of all exponentials in that row. The key difficulty: to know the sum for the row, you need the whole row.
**HBM and SRAM**: a GPU has two main kinds of memory. HBM is the large but relatively slow main memory; SRAM is the much faster but very small on-chip memory.

sections.h: The bottleneck is moving data, not computing

blocks.p: The paper uses the A100 GPU as an example: it has 40–80GB of HBM at 1.5–2.0TB/s, and 108 streaming multiprocessors each with 192KB of SRAM, with estimated bandwidth around 19TB/s. SRAM is an order of magnitude faster, but only about 20MB total—thousands of times smaller than HBM.

callout.title: A warehouse and a workbench
callout.text: HBM is the warehouse: plenty of room for everything, but every trip to fetch something costs time. SRAM is the workbench: instant access, but only a few items fit. The chef (a compute unit) can slice extremely fast; the real time is wasted running between warehouse and workbench.

blocks.p: The paper splits GPU operations into two classes: **compute-bound** ones such as large matrix multiplications, where time depends on how much math is done, and **memory-bound** ones such as elementwise operations, softmax, dropout, and normalization, where time depends on how much data is moved. In attention, the two matrix multiplications are separated by memory-bound steps—softmax, masking, dropout—and all of their inputs and outputs are large N × N matrices.

plain.title: Fast chef, slow errands
plain.text: Some jobs spend most of their time computing, such as multiplying two large matrices (top bar, mostly green). Others spend most of their time moving data, such as softmax: each number needs only a little arithmetic, but it must be fetched from HBM and written back afterward (bottom bar, mostly orange). Attention turns out to be dominated by the second kind.

blocks.p: The standard implementation (Algorithm 0 in the paper) looks like this:

list: Read Q and K from HBM, compute S = QK^{⊺}, and **write S back to HBM**.
Read S from HBM, compute P = softmax(S), and **write P back to HBM**.
Read P and V from HBM, compute O = PV, and write O back to HBM.

plain.title: Don't keep running to the warehouse while cooking
plain.text: A is the standard approach: after each step, you haul the intermediate S and P back to the warehouse (HBM) and carry them out again for the next step. B is FlashAttention: ingredients are brought to the workbench (on-chip SRAM) in batches, the whole dish is prepared there, and only the finished O goes back to the warehouse. Same dish, much less walking.

fig.title: The longer the sequence, the more the attention matrix dominates
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: one attention head with head dimension d = 64. Numbers computed by Lyra-Jade from matrix sizes.
columns: Total entries in Q, K, V, O (4 × N × d)

fig.note: GPT-2 with N = 1024 and d = 64 corresponds to the second row. The inputs and outputs you actually need all grow with N, but the standard implementation writes and reads the N²-sized intermediate matrices several times over.

plain.title: A handshake table is much bigger than a name list
plain.text: With a class of 4, the list has 4 rows, but the "who shook hands with whom" table has 4 × 4 = 16 cells. Double the class to 8 and the list only doubles, but the table becomes 64 cells. The attention matrix is the handshake table: every token is paired with every other token.

sections.h: The hard part: softmax needs the whole row—how do you compute it in blocks?

blocks.p: Tiling is the natural idea; the hard part is softmax. Every weight in a row has to be divided by the sum of exponentials for the whole row, but inside one block you can see only part of it. The paper uses an existing trick called online softmax: as each block is processed, keep two small numbers; when a later block reveals a larger maximum, rescale the previous result accordingly.

parts.desc: The maximum seen so far. Subtracting it before exponentiating prevents overflow.
The running sum of exponentials, relative to m.
Rescaling factor: when the maximum changes, multiply the previous sum by this to switch to the new reference.

formula.note: So carrying just two numbers, (m, ℓ), is enough to compute softmax block by block, and the final result is exactly the same as if the whole row had been seen at once. Output O is corrected with the same factors.

plain.title: Batch accounting, converted on the fly
plain.text: Softmax is like cutting a cake according to scores: to know each person's share, you first need the total number of shares. The list arrives in batches: the first batch has a maximum of 3, so you record 1.14 total shares. The second batch reveals a 5, changing the reference, so you multiply the old total by 0.135 to convert it, then add the new batch's 1.05. The final total is 1.20—exactly what you'd get by seeing the whole list at once.

fig.title: Worked by hand: two blocks produce exactly the same result as one pass
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: one row of attention scores [1, 3, 2, 5] and corresponding values v = [10, 20, 30, 40], split into two blocks. Numbers computed by Lyra-Jade using the formulas in Section 3.1 of the paper.
rows: Merge: multiply block 1 by e^{3−5} = 0.1353, then add
Check: seeing the whole row at once
fig.note: After merging, o = (0.1353 × 1.1353 × 18.81 + 1.0498 × 39.53) ÷ 1.2034 = 36.88, matching the direct computation. That's what exact attention means: not an approximation, just a different order of computation.

blocks.p: With online softmax in hand, the whole algorithm (Algorithm 1 in the paper) is two nested loops:

list: **Outer loop**: split K and V into blocks of size B_{c} and load one K_{j}, V_{j} pair into SRAM at a time.

**Inner loop**: split Q into blocks of size B_{r}, load one block into SRAM, compute S_{ij} = Q_{i} K_{j}^{⊺} together with that block's row maxima and exponential sums, then update the output O_{i} and the statistics (m_{i}, ℓ_{i}) using the correction formulas above and write them back to HBM.
**Block sizes** are set by SRAM capacity M: B_{c} is about M ÷ 4d, ensuring the blocks fit on-chip at the same time.
**One kernel**: matrix multiplication, softmax, masking, dropout, and the final multiplication by V all happen inside a single GPU program, with no intermediate results materialized in HBM.

plain.title: Lay one brick at a time
plain.text: Think of the N × N attention matrix as a wall you need to tile. The outer loop brings the K and V for one column of bricks (top arrow); the inner loop pushes blocks of Q across (left arrow). The workbench holds only the current block (dark green). Each time a block is finished, the corresponding output O on the right is updated (gold). The whole wall never has to be laid out at once.

blocks.p: **What about backprop?** Computing gradients normally needs the two N × N matrices, S and P. FlashAttention doesn't store them. It stores only the output O, the per-row (m, ℓ) statistics, and the state of the random number generator used for dropout. During the backward pass, it recomputes S and P from blocks of Q, K, V on-chip. This adds multiplications, but it eliminates reads and writes of huge matrices, so the backward pass is actually faster.

plain.title: Recomputing beats digging through a filing cabinet
plain.text: Backprop needs earlier large matrices. The standard approach (A) stores them in a distant filing cabinet (HBM) and runs over to look them up when needed. FlashAttention (B) keeps just two small numbers m and ℓ on hand, and recomputes from them on the spot. Pressing a few calculator buttons is much faster than a trip to the archive room.

callout.title: "Less math means faster code"
callout.text: Figure 2 of the paper is a direct counterexample. On GPT-2 medium with sequence length 1024, standard attention uses 66.6 GFLOPs; FlashAttention actually uses more—75.2 GFLOPs—because of recomputation. Yet HBM reads and writes drop from 40.3GB to 4.4GB, and runtime drops from 41.7 ms to 7.3 ms. When an operation is memory-bound, moving less data matters more than doing fewer operations.

blocks.p: The paper also analyzes HBM access volume, or IO complexity, theoretically:

formula.expr: Standard attention: Θ( N d + N^{2} ) HBM accesses; FlashAttention: Θ( N^{2} d^{2} / M ) HBM accesses.

parts.desc: SRAM size. Common d is 64–128 and M is about 100KB, so d² is many times smaller than M, meaning FlashAttention uses many times fewer HBM accesses.
The paper also proves that no exact attention algorithm can asymptotically do better for all SRAM sizes M.

formula.note: Intuition: each trip can move a Θ(M)-sized block of K and V into SRAM, and for every such block you must sweep over all of Q. The larger the SRAM, the fewer sweeps you need.

plain.title: The bigger the cart, the fewer the trips
plain.text: All of Q must be pushed across the workbench again and again. The bigger the workbench (cache M), the more K and V blocks fit in each trip, so fewer trips are needed: for the same job, a small cart makes 6 trips while a big cart makes 2. A larger d² makes each block take up more space, so fewer fit per trip. The paper also proves that no exact algorithm can beat this for every possible workbench size.

blocks.p: Many approximate attention methods let each token look at only some positions. They should save compute, but in practice they are often not much faster because they are also held back by memory traffic. The paper adds a block mask to FlashAttention: masked-out blocks are skipped entirely—not read, not computed.

list: HBM accesses scale by s, the fraction of nonzero blocks, and runtime falls proportionally with sparsity.
It is 2–4× faster than FlashAttention itself and scales to 64K sequence length.
On the Long Range Arena benchmark, it is 2.8× faster than standard attention with comparable accuracy.
Note: this variant is approximate attention; it is no longer exactly the same as the original.

plain.title: Lay only the bricks you need
plain.text: If you decide in advance that many positions don't need to attend to each other, only part of the wall needs brick. On the left, all 36 blocks are laid; on the right, only the 18 dark-green blocks are. The empty cells don't even have material moved into them, so trips and time shrink proportionally. The tradeoff: the result is no longer exactly the same as standard attention.

blocks.p: **BERT-large**: trained on 8 A100 GPUs from the same initialization provided by MLPerf to 72.0% masked-language-model accuracy, averaged over 10 runs:

blocks.p: **GPT-2**: trained on OpenWebText, with the same perplexity (the model definition is unchanged, and the validation curves in the appendix line up) and much shorter training time:

fig.title: GPT-2: same model, training time cut by more than half

blocks.p: **Longer context**: the time and memory saved can be traded for longer sequences. GPT-2 small used FlashAttention to extend context from 1K to 4K and trained in 3.6 days—still about 30% faster than Megatron's 1K baseline (4.7 days)—while perplexity dropped from 18.2 to 17.5.

fig.title: Long-document classification: longer context, higher scores (but only up to a point)
fig.subtitle: From Table 5 of the paper. Micro-averaged F1; higher is better. Columns are sequence lengths.
rows: ECtHR (European Court of Human Rights cases)
fig.note: On MIMIC, 16K is 4.3 points above 512; on ECtHR, 8K is 8.5 points above 512. The “6.4-point lift” in the abstract is the average of these two numbers. MIMIC scores are actually lower at 1024 and 2048 than at 512, and ECtHR at 16K is lower than at 8K; the paper attributes this to differences in document-length distributions.

blocks.p: **Path-X and Path-256**: determine whether two points in a 128×128 (or 256×256) black-and-white image are connected, feeding the image to the model pixel by pixel, giving sequence lengths of 16K and 64K. Previous Transformers either ran out of memory or could only manage coin-flip random guessing. FlashAttention reaches 61.4% on Path-X, and the block-sparse version reaches 63.1% on Path-256.

**Benchmarks**: across common sequence lengths from 128 to 2K, FlashAttention is up to 3× faster than the standard PyTorch implementation and uses up to 20× less memory, with memory footprint growing linearly in sequence length. Approximate attention methods start to overtake it between 512 and 1024, while the block-sparse version is faster than all known implementations at every length. Compared with Apex FMHA, then optimized for short sequences, it is about 4% slower at length 128 and 8% and 5% faster at 256 and 512.

sections.h: Limitations, and a few details worth noting

blocks.p: The limitations the paper lists itself:

list: **Requires hand-written CUDA**: each new attention variant needs a new low-level kernel—a lot of engineering—and it may not port directly to other GPU architectures. The paper hopes such implementations can eventually be compiled automatically from a high-level language like PyTorch.
**Single-GPU only**: moving data between GPUs is another layer of IO, which the paper does not address.

blocks.p: A few things we noticed reading the original:

list: **Inconsistent speedup over Megatron**: the beginning of Section 4 says GPT-2 is 1.8× faster than Megatron, while the Table 2 caption and the main text say 1.7×. Calculated from the days in Table 2, small is 4.7 ÷ 2.7 ≈ 1.7 and medium is 11.5 ÷ 6.9 ≈ 1.7.
**“Up to 3×” is smaller than the number in the table**: the abstract and the Table 2 caption say up to 3× over Hugging Face, but the GPT-2 small row in Table 2 shows 3.5× (9.5 days vs. 2.7 days).

**Path-X's 61.4% includes the effect of extra fine-tuning**: the appendix notes that the best Path-X checkpoint was fine-tuned for another 200 epochs, which gave FlashAttention about 4 percentage points.
**The “6.4-point lift” is an average**: the two datasets are 4.3 and 8.5 points, and scores do not rise monotonically with length (see the table above).
**A subscript typo in Algorithm 1**: line 4 writes the output blocks as O_{i}, ..., O_{T_{r}}, but the first one should be O_{1}; the same issue appears in the ℓ blocks.

sections.h: Afterward: almost the default attention implementation

list: **FlashAttention-2 and -3**: the authors later kept improving parallelization and hardware-specific optimizations for newer GPUs, making it faster still.

**Adoption by mainstream frameworks**: this kind of tiled, fused, never-materialized attention implementation was later widely adopted by mainstream training and inference frameworks, and in many cases users are already using it without changing any code.

**The foundation for long context**: linear memory growth was one of the engineering prerequisites that let model context grow from a few thousand to hundreds of thousands of tokens. Paired with the RoPE extrapolation method from the previous article, long context became truly usable.

**The IO-aware mindset**: the paper's emphasis on figuring out how data moves before optimizing influenced a great deal of later inference optimization work, such as PagedAttention in this site's reading list, which manages the KV cache.

**Same author, another path**: first author Tri Dao later became one of the authors of Mamba, which tries to bypass attention's quadratic complexity structurally; it is the 11th article in this series.

blocks.p: The next article looks at another inference bottleneck: **GQA, grouped-query attention**. It lets several attention heads share the same keys and values, cutting a large chunk of the KV cache that inference must repeatedly read.

quiz.q: How does FlashAttention's output compare with standard attention?
options: It is approximate, with very small error.
Exactly the same; only the order of computation and the pattern of HBM reads and writes differ.
More accurate, because it uses higher precision.
quiz.why: FlashAttention is exact attention: after tiling and online-softmax correction, it is mathematically identical to computing it in one shot. Only the block-sparse version is approximate.

quiz.q: FlashAttention actually does a bit more computation than standard attention—why is it faster?
options: Because it runs on a faster GPU.
Because attention is memory-bound: it keeps the N × N matrix in on-chip cache and reduces HBM reads and writes by about 9×.
Because it uses lower numerical precision.
quiz.why: Figure 2 of the paper: GFLOPs rise from 66.6 to 75.2, but HBM reads and writes drop from 40.3GB to 4.4GB and time drops from 41.7 ms to 7.3 ms.

quiz.q: Why do you need to keep track of each row's maximum m and exponential sum ℓ when computing softmax block by block?
options: Because a later block may contain a larger value, and these two numbers let you rescale the previous partial result accordingly.
quiz.why: The denominator of softmax is the exponential sum for the entire row. As long as you remember (m, ℓ), when a new block arrives you can multiply the old result by e^{old m - new m} to correct it, ending up exactly as if you had seen the whole row at once.

blocks.p: After reading this piece, you should be able to answer these questions:

list: Why is attention's bottleneck data movement rather than computation? How do HBM and SRAM differ?
Which large matrices does standard attention write to HBM, and why do they grow quadratically with sequence length?
How does online softmax assemble the block results into the exact result?
In the backward pass, why does FlashAttention prefer recomputation over storing the attention matrix?
Among the paper's speedup numbers, which refer to end-to-end training and which refer to attention alone?
